item.text: {"question_id":"1B.2","answer":"During 2023, Xi-led China publicly used restrained nuclear language: it stated that nuclear weapons must not be used or threatened, nuclear war cannot be won, and parties should exercise restraint and avoid attacks on nuclear facilities (BATCH-0015-E005; BATCH-0013-E005; BATCH-0018-E008). China also reaffirmed no-first-use, minimum deterrence, and negative security assurances (BATCH-0017-E002; BATCH-0023-E001; BATCH-0025-E016). These are direct official representations, but they do not by themselves establish implementation or operational corroboration. The inherited and continuing posture provides some corroboration: nuclear launch or alert decisions were reportedly concentrated in top civilian institutions, warheads were generally stored separately from delivery systems, and forces were kept at low peacetime readiness (BATCH-0016-E007; BATCH-0017-E008; BATCH-0025-E029). However, modernization since about 2019 increased arsenal size, readiness, diversity, and silo deployment; analysts identified possible future launch-on-warning implications, while finding no clear decision that such a posture had been adopted (BATCH-0005-E006; BATCH-0025-E028; BATCH-0025-E029). The supplied evidence therefore supports responsible declaratory nuclear rhetoric and some inherited control safeguards, but leaves a material, unresolved gap between rhetoric and the modernization-era operational posture. Taiwan and maritime warnings show coercive conventional rhetoric, but do not establish nuclear threats, brinkmanship, or apocalyptic language and should not be treated as direct evidence for this question (BATCH-0005-E011; BATCH-0024-E006; BATCH-0019-E001).","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0015-E005","BATCH-0013-E005","BATCH-0018-E008","BATCH-0017-E002","BATCH-0023-E001","BATCH-0025-E016","BATCH-0016-E007","BATCH-0017-E008"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0005-E006","BATCH-0025-E028","BATCH-0025-E029","BATCH-0005-E011","BATCH-0024-E006","BATCH-0019-E001"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied operational evidence is open-source, partly inferential, and does not provide a complete 2023 doctrine, command-order record, or independent inspection of safeguards.","The inherited-control evidence predates or spans the target period and does not prove that all arrangements remained unchanged during modernization.","The evidence does not establish that China adopted launch-on-warning, shifted to first use, or issued nuclear threats during 2023.","Most favorable evidence is official declaratory material; implementation and consistency with operational posture remain independently under-verified."],"corrections_made":["Reduced the claim from comparatively responsible rhetoric to responsible declaratory rhetoric, explicitly distinguishing official statements from verified conduct.","Removed Taiwan and maritime warnings as direct evidence of a nuclear posture gap; retained them only as contextual conventional coercion evidence.","Added the inherited centralized-control, separated-storage, and low-peacetime-readiness baseline.","Reframed modernization and launch-on-warning evidence as an unresolved operational contradiction or gap, not proof of adopted nuclear brinkmanship.","Preserved the period, attribution limits, source limitations, and uncertainty."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A complete judgment would benefit from dated 2023 evidence on formal nuclear doctrine, alert status, warhead handling, launch authority, and operational orders.","Independent corroboration is needed to determine whether modernization materially changed the relationship between declaratory no-first-use policy and operational posture."]}
